result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.is_valid_coloring()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Check if a coloring is valid (no adjacent nodes share a color). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L43291-L43368){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.is_valid_coloring(coloring) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Is valid coloring](/assets/graphs/is-valid-coloring.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The same two-by-three ladder on both sides, each node filled with its color and badged with the color number. Left: no edge joins two nodes of the same color, so is_valid_coloring() returns True. Right: F is recolored to 2, the same color as its neighbor C, and that edge (shown in the accent color) makes is_valid_coloring() return False." width="100%"} A (proper) vertex coloring gives each node a color such that the two endpoints of every edge have different colors. This method walks over every edge and returns `False` as soon as it finds one whose endpoints share a color. Use it to verify a coloring that came from somewhere other than `greedy_color()`: one built by hand, loaded from a file, produced by another tool, or modified after the fact (for example, after merging two color classes to reduce the number of time slots in a schedule). A few details of the check: - edge direction is ignored, so `A -> B` forbids `A` and `B` from sharing a color - self-loops are ignored (a node is never in conflict with itself) - nodes missing from `coloring=` are skipped, so a *partial* coloring is reported as valid when none of its colored nodes conflict; it does not check that every node is colored - keys that are not node IDs in the graph are ignored ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [coloring]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [dict[int, int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A dictionary mapping integer node IDs to integer colors, such as the output of `greedy_color()`. Colors can be any integers; only equality between the colors of adjacent nodes matters. Keys must be node IDs, not labels. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `True` if no edge joins two nodes of the same color, `False` otherwise. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} On a path `A-B-C`, alternating colors between neighbors produces a valid coloring. Building the dictionary from label lookups keeps the node IDs straight: ::: {#a7015019 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")]) ) a, b, c = (graph.get_id_from_label(x) for x in ["A", "B", "C"]) # Valid coloring (alternating colors) valid = {a: 0, b: 1, c: 0} # Returns True graph.is_valid_coloring(valid) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` True ``` ::: ::: Assigning the same color to two adjacent nodes (`A` and `B`) makes the coloring invalid: ::: {#4a222db2 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Invalid coloring (adjacent nodes share a color) invalid = {a: 0, b: 0, c: 1} # Returns False graph.is_valid_coloring(invalid) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` False ``` ::: ::: Only colored nodes are checked, so a partial coloring that leaves out `C` still passes. The output of `greedy_color()` is always valid: ::: {#994f68b8 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} (graph.is_valid_coloring({a: 0, b: 1}), graph.is_valid_coloring(graph.greedy_color())) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (True, True) ``` ::: :::
